target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would directly solve scheduling barriers to voting.
objection: A federal Election Day holiday would not automatically fix the schedule problem because private employers are not required to give paid time off; many low-income workers in retail, restaurants, caregiving, and other hourly service jobs would still be scheduled to work and could face a choice between losing wages and voting.

target: AG2’s objection that low-income workers would still be stuck working because a holiday is unenforceable.
objection: The objection assumes a holiday must be only symbolic. In fact, lawmakers could pair a federal Election Day holiday with enforceable voting-time protections, such as guaranteed time to vote or protected leave, which would remove the inequity concern.

target: AG1’s rebuttal that enforcement can be added so the holiday would not disadvantage low-income workers.
objection: Even if a holiday exists, federal holidays do not by themselves compel private employers to give paid leave, so many hourly workers would still be scheduled and still have to choose between voting and losing wages; therefore the holiday alone does not reliably solve the scheduling barrier.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday leaves low-income workers with no usable time to vote.
objection: Declaring Election Day a holiday changes the default environment: schools close, consumer activity drops, and many employers reduce hours or close, so more workers actually gain usable non-working time to vote even without a paid-leave mandate.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday will reduce schedule barriers for constrained workers.
objection: A federal holiday may alter some school and workplace schedules, but it does not require private employers to close or provide paid leave, so many essential service and customer-facing jobs will still run and still schedule hourly workers; for them, the holiday may not create real non-working time.

target: AG2’s assumption that most low-income workers will still be effectively working on a holiday.
objection: The assumption overstates how unchanged private scheduling remains. A federally recognized holiday changes baseline conditions, prompting many employers to close or reduce staffing because schools, childcare, public transit, and consumer demand also shift, which creates usable time off for a substantial share of hourly workers.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday broadly creates usable non-working time.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or to provide paid leave, so holiday status will not consistently convert into actual time off for low-income hourly workers; the burden can remain deciding between lost wages and voting.

target: AG2’s assumption that holiday status leaves hourly workers unchanged.
objection: That assumption ignores how a national holiday changes scheduling norms and demand conditions. Many employers in retail, food service, and similar sectors will reduce hours or close, so a substantial portion of hourly workers will gain non-working time and the schedule barrier will be reduced.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday “moves voting off the ordinary school/work calendar” for constrained workers.
objection: A federal Election Day holiday does not reliably move voting off the work calendar for low-income workers because private employers are not required to close or provide paid time off, so the lost-wages-versus-voting tradeoff can remain.

target: AG1’s claim that Election Day as a holiday is an effective turnout reform.
objection: As a standalone reform, an election-day holiday is not an effective way to increase turnout compared with more direct access reforms like automatic voter registration or employer time-off requirements, because holidays are only an indirect convenience nudge.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is only a crude or symbolic lever for turnout.
objection: A national holiday directly changes the practical time constraints that suppress turnout: it moves Election Day off a normal school/work day, reduces scheduling conflicts, and signals voting as a civic celebration, which can lower friction and raise participation.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday will give constrained workers usable time off.
objection: The key weak assumption is that constrained workers will actually have the day off in practice; because private employers are not required to close or provide paid leave, many hourly workers may still be scheduled and still face lost wages if they vote.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is just a mild convenience measure.
objection: The holiday is more than a convenience nudge because it directly targets a major turnout blocker: conflicts with school and work schedules. By changing default operating conditions, it expands the pool of voters with non-working time to vote and can therefore meaningfully raise turnout.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday broadly raises turnout by reducing schedule barriers.
objection: That causal chain depends on most low-income hourly workers actually getting usable non-working time without wage loss, but a federal holiday does not compel private employers to close or provide paid leave, so the holiday can still leave those workers with the same tradeoff between wages and voting.

target: AG2’s claim that the turnout effect would be limited or mostly symbolic.
objection: The holiday directly alters the real-world time constraints that keep people from voting by giving them a day off from the normal school/work calendar, which makes the policy an effective turnout-supporting reform rather than just an abstract nudge.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday will shift operating conditions enough to help low-income hourly workers.
objection: That assumption is weak because a federal holiday does not require private employers to close or to provide paid time off, so many shift-based workplaces can remain open and continue scheduling employees, leaving the work-schedule barrier intact for low-income workers.

target: AG2’s objection that a holiday only offers convenience and does not meaningfully change barriers.
objection: A national Election Day holiday is not merely a convenience measure; it directly changes the schedule conditions that create barriers by freeing voters from normal school/work obligations and giving them non-school, non-work time to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status broadly reduces time-budget pressure on voters.
objection: The claimed causal chain fails for the people most constrained by work schedules, because a federal holiday is not a mandate on private employers; many essential customer-facing workplaces can stay open and keep workers on schedule, so the holiday does not reliably translate into time to vote without wage loss.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is only a symbolic convenience and does not meaningfully improve access.
objection: A national Election Day holiday directly targets the main practical barrier—conflicts with work and school schedules—by changing the default operating conditions and expanding the number of people who can vote without missing work or school or losing pay.
